title: Sleep for Recovery
content: 7-9 hours of sleep is critical for recovery. Growth hormone is primarily released during deep sleep. Less than 6 hours impairs recovery, performance, and increases injury risk. Consistent sleep schedule improves sleep quality. Cool room (18-20C), no screens before bed, no caffeine after 2PM. Athletes should aim for 8-10 hours.

title: Rest Days
content: Rest days allow muscle repair and nervous system recovery. Most lifters need 1-3 rest days per week depending on intensity and volume. Active recovery (light walking, stretching, yoga) is beneficial. Complete rest is sometimes needed if overtrained. Signs of needing rest: persistent fatigue, decreased performance, joint pain, poor sleep, elevated resting heart rate.

title: Muscle Soreness (DOMS)
content: DOMS (Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness) peaks 24-72 hours post-workout. It's caused by micro-damage to muscle fibers during eccentric loading. Management: light movement, foam rolling, adequate protein (1.6-2.2g/kg), sleep, hydration. Being sore doesn't mean a workout was effective - progressive overload matters more. Soreness decreases with training adaptation.

title: Foam Rolling and Recovery
content: Foam rolling can reduce DOMS perception modestly. Use 1-2 minutes per muscle group, avoid rolling joints directly. Apply moderate pressure - it shouldn't be extremely painful. Best used post-workout or on rest days. Not a substitute for adequate sleep, nutrition, and programming.

title: Stretching and Mobility
content: Dynamic stretching before training improves range of motion and performance. Static stretching post-training or on rest days improves long-term flexibility. Hold static stretches 30 seconds for 2-4 sets. Don't static stretch cold muscles before heavy lifting - it may reduce force output. Daily mobility work (10 minutes) is more effective than occasional long sessions.

title: Overtraining Signs and Prevention
content: Overtraining syndrome includes: persistent fatigue, decreased performance, elevated resting heart rate, frequent illness, mood changes, sleep disturbances, decreased motivation. Prevention: adequate recovery (sleep, rest days), gradual volume progression, deload weeks every 4-8 weeks. Treatment: reduce training load, increase sleep, address nutritional deficiencies.
